title: LATERAL joins, top-N per group and keyset pagination
goal: By the end you can write a subquery in FROM that runs once per row of the tables before it (LATERAL), choose between a window filter, LATERAL with LIMIT and DISTINCT ON for the top N rows per group, and page through a large table with a keyset cursor that stays fast on page 5,001.

warmup.q: An admin screen lists 1,000,000 payments newest first, 20 per page, and an index on (created_at, payment_id) matches that order. Page 5,001 uses `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000`. About how many index entries does PostgreSQL read?
options: 20: the index lets it jump straight to entry 100,001
About 100,020
About 40: one descent of the index, then 20 entries
warmup.why: An index is sorted, but it does not store row numbers, so there is nothing to jump to. OFFSET makes PostgreSQL read the first 100,000 entries in order, throw them away, and return the next 20. On the large data set that is 100,020 rows and 2,865 buffers. The last option describes a keyset cursor, which seeks to the last row of the previous page instead of counting.

sections.h: A subquery in FROM cannot see the row beside it, and LATERAL lets it
sections.body:
The merchant dashboard shows each merchant with its three largest succeeded payments. The question is per merchant: for every merchant row, a small query that depends on that merchant.

The first attempt puts the small query in FROM, as a derived table (lesson 5), and refers to the merchant inside it:

```sql
SELECT m.merchant_id, t.payment_id, t.amount_minor
FROM merchants m
CROSS JOIN (SELECT payment_id, amount_minor
            FROM payments p
            WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND p.status = 'succeeded'
            ORDER BY amount_minor DESC, payment_id
            LIMIT 3) AS t;
```

PostgreSQL rejects it, and its hint names the fix:

```postgresql
ERROR:  invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "m"
DETAIL:  There is an entry for table "m", but it cannot be referenced from this part of the query.
HINT:  To reference that table, you must mark this subquery with LATERAL.
```

Items in FROM are independent: each is computed on its own, and then they are joined. So the subquery may not mention `m`, and without that condition it returns the three largest payments overall. A scalar subquery in the select list (lesson 5) may mention `m`, because it is correlated, but it must return one value, and three payments fail with `more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression`.

The keyword `LATERAL` in front of a subquery in FROM lets it refer to the FROM items to its left. PostgreSQL then runs it once for each row of those items, with that row's values plugged in, and joins each row to whatever rows its run returned. Write `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (...)` in the query above and it works. A LATERAL subquery is a correlated subquery that returns rows instead of one value. In Kotlin it is a flatMap:

```kotlin
merchants.flatMap { m ->
    payments.filter { it.merchantId == m.id && it.status == "succeeded" }
        .sortedWith(compareByDescending<Payment> { it.amountMinor }.thenBy { it.paymentId })
        .take(3)
        .map { m to it }                     // join each returned row to its merchant
}
```

That is the picture for this lesson: **for each outer row, run the inner query with that row's values, and join the rows it returns.** The stepper runs it merchant by merchant.

The result has 18 rows for 6 merchants. Paper Lantern Books (6) and Sunrise Grocers (8) are missing: their runs returned nothing, and CROSS JOIN, like an inner join (lesson 3), drops a row with no partner. `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) AS t ON true` keeps them, with NULLs. The `ON true` is there only because LEFT JOIN needs an ON clause; the subquery has already done the matching.

You may have used LATERAL without the keyword. A function call in FROM can always use earlier columns, so `CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(p.metadata -> 'risk' -> 'rules') AS r (rule)` turns each payment's list of fired risk rules into one row per rule.

sections.h: Top N per group, three ways, and what each does with ties
sections.body:
The dashboard query is one case of a pattern you will write often: the top N rows of each group. The newest payment per card, the three biggest merchants per country, the latest login per customer. PostgreSQL gives you three ways to write it. They differ in what they do with ties, in which groups appear, and in cost.

The window way, from lesson 7, numbers the rows inside each group and keeps the first N one level up:

```sql
SELECT merchant_id, payment_id, amount_minor
FROM (SELECT merchant_id, payment_id, amount_minor,
             row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id
                                ORDER BY amount_minor DESC, payment_id) AS place
      FROM payments
      WHERE status = 'succeeded') AS ranked
WHERE place <= 3;
```

The LATERAL way, from the first section, runs one small query per merchant with LIMIT 3.

The DISTINCT ON way works for N = 1. `SELECT DISTINCT ON (merchant_id) ...` keeps the first row of each set of rows with equal merchant_id, where "first" means first in the query's ORDER BY. So the ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON columns and continue with whatever decides the winner: `ORDER BY merchant_id, amount_minor DESC, payment_id`. Start it with anything else and PostgreSQL refuses: `SELECT DISTINCT ON expressions must match initial ORDER BY expressions`. DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL's own syntax, not standard SQL, and it is the shortest way to write "the latest row per key".

The three agree only if they agree on ties. Metro Transit (merchant 3) has one 5.50 ride and three 2.75 rides, so its top three cut through a tie: 550, then two of the three 275s. With `payment_id` as the tiebreaker, row_number and LIMIT both keep payments 4 and 9 and drop 26. Without it, which 275 survives is up to the plan. If tied rows should all stay, filter on `rank() <= 3`, which gives Metro Transit four rows, or write `FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS WITH TIES` inside the LATERAL subquery (lesson 1). Decide first, because none of the three fails when you forget: each one quietly keeps whichever rows the plan delivers first.

They also differ in which groups appear. The window and DISTINCT ON ways start from payments, so a merchant without payments has no rows to number and never appears. The LATERAL way starts from merchants, so LEFT JOIN LATERAL can keep every merchant. When the dashboard must list every merchant, start from the merchants table.

sections.h: Which way is fast depends on the index
sections.body:
On 37 payments all three ways finish in a few milliseconds at most. On the large data set, a million payments at 2,500 merchants, they behave very differently, and the reason is how many rows each has to read.

The window way reads every succeeded payment, 930,826 rows, and sorts them all by merchant and amount before row_number can count. It does that work whether you want the top 3 or the top 300. It takes about 1 to 3 seconds on a laptop.

The LATERAL way runs its small query 2,500 times. With no help, each run reads the whole payments table to find one merchant's rows, then sorts them: 20 merchants took about 4 to 9 seconds, so all 2,500 would take many minutes. This is lesson 5's correlated subquery problem again: an inner query that runs once per outer row, and is a full table scan every time.

An index changes that. Lesson 11 builds indexes up properly. For now, an **index** is a separate structure that keeps chosen columns sorted, each entry with a pointer to its row. With an index on `(merchant_id, amount_minor DESC, payment_id)`, each merchant's payments sit next to each other in exactly the order the subquery wants. "The three largest payments of merchant 1000" becomes: find merchant 1000's first entry, read three entries, follow three pointers. EXPLAIN shows it as a Nested Loop over the 2,500 merchants with an Index Scan inside, `rows=3.00 loops=2500`. The whole query took between 0.04 and 0.7 seconds, depending on whether the index was already in memory.

So the rule of thumb: when the groups are big, you want a few rows from each, and an index matches the inner ORDER BY, use LATERAL with LIMIT. When there is no such index, or you need most of each group anyway, the window's single big sort is the cheaper way. Look at the plan before you decide.

One more measurement from the same session is worth knowing. With the index in place, the planner chose to feed the window version from the index too, to skip the sort, and it got slower: 5 to 10 seconds. Reading a whole table through an index visits the table's pages in index order, one row at a time, while a sequential scan reads them in order and the sort runs in memory and temporary files. An index helps when it lets you read less. When you have to read everything, reading the table in its own order and sorting is often faster.

sections.h: OFFSET reads every row it skips
sections.body:
The admin console lists payments newest first, 20 per page, with page numbers at the bottom. The obvious query for page n uses LIMIT and OFFSET:

```sql
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;          -- page 5,001
```

OFFSET 100000 means "skip the first 100,000 rows of the result". To skip a row, PostgreSQL has to produce it first; the documentation says the rows skipped by OFFSET still have to be computed inside the server. An index does not store row numbers, so there is no way to jump to the 100,001st entry. With an index on `(created_at, payment_id)`, page 1 reads the newest 20 entries and stops: 5 buffers (a buffer is one 8 KB page) and a fraction of a millisecond. Page 5,001 walks the index from the newest entry through 100,020 entries, fetches each row, throws away 100,000 and returns 20: 2,865 buffers and about 50 ms. Page 45,001 read 900,020 rows and took 1.2 seconds. The cost grows with the page number, and without the index it is worse: every page sorts the whole table.

OFFSET is also wrong when rows arrive while someone pages, and in a payments system rows always arrive. Page 1 shows payments 37 to 33. A new payment comes in. Page 2, OFFSET 5, now starts one row earlier than it would have, so it shows payment 33 a second time. A deleted row does the opposite, and the next page skips a row nobody saw. An export job that pages with OFFSET can process a payment twice or miss one, and no error says so.

The figure shows both queries on the same index. The OFFSET query reads its way to the page. The second query, from the next section, jumps there.

The fix is to stop counting rows. The client already knows where the last page ended: the last row it showed. Ask for the rows after that row.

sections.h: Keyset pagination starts after the last row you sent
sections.body:
Send the client a cursor: the sort key of the last row on the page, here its created_at and payment_id. For the next page, ask for the rows that come after that key in the sort order:

```sql
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE (created_at, payment_id) < (:last_created_at, :last_payment_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

`(a, b) < (x, y)` is a **row comparison**; lesson 5 used one with `=`. With `<`, PostgreSQL compares the pairs left to right and stops at the first pair that differs, the way Kotlin's `compareBy({ it.createdAt }, { it.paymentId })` does. A payment comes before the cursor if its created_at is earlier, or if the created_at is equal and its payment_id is smaller. Because the order is descending, "before" in value means "after" on the screen.

This is **keyset pagination**, also called the seek method. With the index on `(created_at, payment_id)`, PostgreSQL descends the index once to the cursor's position and reads the next 20 entries. That is the same work on page 2 and on page 5,001: EXPLAIN shows the row comparison as an `Index Cond` and 5 buffers, about a millisecond or less, where OFFSET needed 2,865. New payments shift nothing: they sort before the cursor and show up on page 1.

Three details decide whether it is correct. The ORDER BY must be unique, which is why payment_id is in it: two payments in the same microsecond are rare in a test and normal in a batch. The WHERE must use the whole row comparison: `WHERE created_at < :last_created_at` alone skips every remaining payment that shares the cursor's created_at, silently. And the ORDER BY, the row comparison and the index must agree in column order and direction. Mixed directions, such as created_at DESC with payment_id ASC, cannot be written as one row comparison.

The spelled-out form `created_at < :t OR (created_at = :t AND payment_id < :id)` returns the same rows, but PostgreSQL 18 did not seek with it. EXPLAIN showed it as a Filter that read and threw away 100,000 index entries, as many as OFFSET. So write the row comparison.

You give up page numbers. A cursor moves forward one page at a time, and backward if you flip the comparison and the sort, but it cannot jump to page 4,000. For an infinite scroll, an API with a `next` token or a batch export, that costs nothing. Return the cursor to API clients as an opaque token, for example the two values in base64, so they cannot build their own and come to depend on its format.

refs.title: Use The Index, Luke: Paging through results

analogy: LATERAL is a receptionist working down a list of guests. For each guest, she phones their floor and asks for that guest's three newest messages, writes them next to the name, and moves on; a guest with no messages either gets crossed off the list (CROSS JOIN) or keeps a blank line (LEFT JOIN). OFFSET pagination is reading a phone book to someone page by page by counting lines from the first page every time: to read page 500 you count through 499 pages. A keyset cursor is a bookmark with the last name you read: you open the book at that name, which the alphabetical order lets you find directly, and read on. The analogy breaks for the receptionist: PostgreSQL does not always phone each floor. Without LATERAL in the query it is free to plan a join any way it likes, and even with LATERAL a cheap index is what makes each call quick.
in_your_world: The N+1 query is the most common performance bug in JVM services: load 100 merchants, then call the database once per merchant for its latest payment, from a Kotlin loop or a JPA lazy collection. A LEFT JOIN LATERAL does the same per-row lookup inside one statement, one round trip instead of 101, with the same index doing the work. Keyset pagination is what every list endpoint and every batch export over payments, ledger entries or Kafka-outbox rows should use: a REST API returns a `next` cursor, a Temporal activity that exports a table in chunks stores the last key in its heartbeat details so a retry resumes where it stopped, and nothing is processed twice when new rows arrive mid-export. In Oracle the same per-row subquery is written with LATERAL or CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY, all three since 12c.
mistake: Paginating with OFFSET because the UI has page numbers, or because the ORM makes it one call (`PageRequest.of(page, size)`). It looks fine in development with a few hundred rows. In production, deep pages get slower in proportion to the page number, crawlers and export jobs request exactly those pages, and rows inserted between requests shift every page, so exports duplicate or drop rows. The second most common mistake is a keyset cursor on a non-unique column: `WHERE created_at < :last` skips any row that shares the last row's timestamp, which batch inserts guarantee. Paginate with a cursor over a unique sort key, `(created_at, id)`, compare it with a row comparison, and back it with an index in the same column order.

compare.title: The next page with a keyset cursor: Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle 12c and later
a.src:
-- Oracle cannot apply < to a row value (ORA-01796),
-- so the cursor is spelled out: a range the index can
-- use, minus the rows already shown
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE created_at <= :last_created_at
  AND NOT (created_at = :last_created_at
           AND payment_id >= :last_payment_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.src:
-- one row comparison: the whole cursor is the
-- Index Cond of a single index scan
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE (created_at, payment_id)
      < (:last_created_at, :last_payment_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
LIMIT 20;           -- FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY also works

compare.note: Both return the same page. Use The Index, Luke reports that Oracle supports row values but cannot apply range operators to them, failing with ORA-01796, and gives the left-hand form as the workaround: `created_at <= :t` is a plain range on the index's first column, so the index can seek to the cursor's timestamp, and the NOT removes the few rows at that timestamp that were already shown. PostgreSQL can use a row comparison directly as an index condition, so one condition says it. `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` is the standard spelling of LIMIT and works in both; old Oracle code pages with nested ROWNUM queries instead. For the per-row subqueries of this lesson, Oracle 12c added LATERAL inline views and CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY joins; OUTER APPLY is PostgreSQL's LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true.

worked.title: From N+1 queries to one: the latest payment for every merchant

steps.say: The dashboard service loads the merchants, then asks for each merchant's latest succeeded payment, one query per merchant. That is 1 + N round trips: 9 on the seed, 2,501 on the large data set, each paying the network latency between the service and the database.

The loop body is the LATERAL subquery. The `?` becomes `m.merchant_id`, the loop becomes the outer table, and LEFT JOIN with `ON true` keeps the merchants whose query found nothing, as the Kotlin code kept them with a null.
steps.code:
-- 2. the loop body, moved into the statement
SELECT m.merchant_id, m.name, last.payment_id, last.amount_minor, last.created_at
FROM merchants m
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount_minor, p.created_at
    FROM payments p
    WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND p.status = 'succeeded'
    ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.payment_id DESC
    LIMIT 1
) AS last ON true

steps.say: The dashboard also wants each merchant's number of succeeded payments in June. A second LATERAL can compute it. An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, even over no rows (count is then 0), so CROSS JOIN is safe here and drops no merchant.
steps.code:
-- 3. a second per-merchant subquery: one aggregate row each
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT count(*) AS payments_30d
    FROM payments p
    WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND p.status = 'succeeded'
      AND p.created_at >= timestamptz '2026-07-01' - interval '30 days'
      AND p.created_at <  timestamptz '2026-07-01'
) AS recent
ORDER BY m.merchant_id;   -- and add recent.payments_30d to the SELECT list

steps.say: One statement, one round trip, all eight merchants. On the large data set the same statement is 2,500 index lookups inside the database instead of 2,501 network round trips, given an index on `(merchant_id, created_at, payment_id)` for the inner ORDER BY.

drill.title: A keyset page for one card, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the query for the next page of card 8's payments, newest first, 20 per page, after a page that ended with payment 18 (created 2026-03-12 16:42:10 UTC). Then write the index that lets PostgreSQL seek straight to the cursor.

answer.src:
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE card_id = 8                                                      -- the group being paged
  AND (created_at, payment_id) < (timestamptz '2026-03-12 16:42:10+00', 18)   -- after the cursor
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC                              -- unique, same columns and direction
LIMIT 20;
-- 17 | 2026-03-12 16:40:00+00 | 18999
--  6 | 2026-01-22 12:05:00+00 |  2150

-- equality column first, then the sort key in the same order; read backward for DESC
CREATE INDEX payments_card_created_idx ON payments (card_id, created_at, payment_id);

recap: LATERAL lets a subquery in FROM use columns of the FROM items to its left. PostgreSQL runs it once per such row and joins each row to what its run returned.
CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops rows whose run returned nothing. LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true keeps them with NULLs.
Top N per group: row_number in a subquery, LATERAL with LIMIT, or DISTINCT ON for N = 1. Decide what ties mean and say it with a tiebreaker, rank or WITH TIES.
LATERAL with LIMIT is fast when an index matches its ORDER BY: a few index entries per group. Without one, the window's single sort is cheaper.

OFFSET reads and discards every skipped row and shifts when rows arrive. Keyset pagination seeks past the last row sent with a row comparison on a unique sort key, backed by an index in the same order.

quiz.q: The dashboard must list every merchant with its single largest payment, including merchants with no payments. Which FROM clause does that?
options: `merchants m CROSS JOIN LATERAL (... WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id ORDER BY amount_minor DESC LIMIT 1) t`
`merchants m LEFT JOIN LATERAL (... WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id ORDER BY amount_minor DESC LIMIT 1) t ON true`
`(SELECT DISTINCT ON (merchant_id) ... FROM payments ORDER BY merchant_id, amount_minor DESC) t`
`merchants m JOIN (SELECT ... FROM payments ORDER BY amount_minor DESC LIMIT 1) t ON t.merchant_id = m.merchant_id`
quiz.why: LEFT JOIN LATERAL runs the subquery per merchant and keeps a merchant whose run returned nothing. CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops it. DISTINCT ON starts from payments, so merchants without payments never appear. The last one takes the single largest payment overall and joins one merchant to it.

quiz.q: Which payment per card does `SELECT DISTINCT ON (card_id) card_id, payment_id FROM payments ORDER BY card_id, created_at` return?
options: The card's latest payment
An arbitrary payment, because DISTINCT ON ignores ORDER BY
The card's earliest payment
None: it fails without DESC
quiz.why: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each card in the ORDER BY, and `created_at` ascending puts the earliest first. For the latest, write `ORDER BY card_id, created_at DESC, payment_id DESC`; the payment_id makes the winner fixed when two payments share a time.

quiz.q: A page ended with the payment (created_at 10:00:00, id 500). The next page uses `WHERE created_at < '10:00:00' ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC LIMIT 20`. Payments 498 and 499 were also created at 10:00:00. What happens to them?
options: They appear first on the next page
They appear on the next page in random order
The query fails because created_at is not unique
They are never shown: the condition excludes every row at 10:00:00
quiz.why: Comparing created_at alone treats the whole timestamp as seen, so rows that tie with the cursor but sort after it are skipped for good. `(created_at, payment_id) < ('10:00:00', 500)` includes them, because for equal times it compares the ids.

quiz.q: With an index on (created_at, payment_id), why does `ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` still read 100,020 index entries?
options: The index keeps entries sorted but stores no positions, so PostgreSQL must count its way to entry 100,001
OFFSET disables the use of indexes
PostgreSQL locks the skipped rows first
The planner cannot read an index backward
quiz.why: An index can find a key quickly; it cannot find a position. OFFSET is a position, so the scan starts at the newest entry and counts. The plan in the Try it used the index, backward, and still read 100,020 rows. A keyset condition gives the scan a key to seek to instead.

quiz.q: Lesson 5 showed a correlated subquery as a SubPlan that runs once per outer row. How does a LATERAL subquery relate to it?
options: It is uncorrelated and runs once, like an InitPlan
It is a correlated subquery placed in FROM: it runs per row of the items to its left and may return many rows and columns
PostgreSQL always turns it into a hash join
It can return only one row, like a scalar subquery
quiz.why: Both are correlated: they read values from an outer row. A scalar subquery must return one value; a LATERAL subquery returns a table, joined to the row it was run for. Like the SubPlan in lesson 5, it is cheap when each run uses an index and expensive when each run scans a big table.

flashcards.back: A subquery in FROM may use columns of the FROM items to its left. PostgreSQL runs it once per such row.

flashcards.front: CROSS JOIN LATERAL or LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true?
flashcards.back: CROSS drops outer rows whose run returned nothing. LEFT keeps them with NULLs; ON true is required syntax.

flashcards.front: What must the ORDER BY of a DISTINCT ON query start with?
flashcards.back: The DISTINCT ON expressions. The columns after them decide which row of each group is kept.

flashcards.front: Three ways to get the top N rows per group?
flashcards.back: row_number() in a subquery with `WHERE place <= N`; LATERAL with ORDER BY and LIMIT N; DISTINCT ON for N = 1.

flashcards.front: Why is OFFSET slow on deep pages?
flashcards.back: Skipped rows are still produced and thrown away: page 5,001 of 20 reads 100,020 rows. An index stores keys, not positions.

flashcards.front: What is the keyset condition for the next page, newest first?
flashcards.back: `WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n`, with an index on (created_at, id).

flashcards.front: Why must a keyset cursor include a unique column?
flashcards.back: Without it, rows that tie with the cursor's value are skipped or repeated. The unique column makes every position exact.

terms.plain: A keyword that lets a subquery in FROM refer to earlier FROM items; it runs once per row of them.
The first N rows of each group in some order, such as each merchant's three largest payments.
PostgreSQL syntax that keeps the first row, by ORDER BY, of each set of rows with equal values.
Skips the first n rows of a result. The skipped rows are still produced.
Paging by remembering the sort key of the last row sent and asking for rows after it. Also called the seek method.
The last row's sort key, handed to the client as a token for the next page.
`(a, b) < (x, y)`: compares pairs left to right and stops at the first pair that differs.
A separate structure that keeps chosen columns sorted with a pointer to each row. Lesson 11 builds it up.

explain_back.prompt: A nightly export pages through a 50-million-row ledger_entries table with `ORDER BY entry_id LIMIT 1000 OFFSET :n`. It gets slower every hour and sometimes exports an entry twice. Explain both symptoms and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: OFFSET does not jump: to skip n rows PostgreSQL has to produce them, so batch k reads about k times 1,000 index entries and throws all but the last 1,000 away. The total work grows with the square of the number of batches, which is why each hour is slower than the last. The duplicates come from rows that change while the export runs. OFFSET counts positions, so an entry inserted with a lower entry_id after a batch was read pushes every later row one position down, and the next batch starts with the last row of the previous one; a deleted row does the opposite and one row is skipped. The fix is keyset pagination: remember the last entry_id of each batch and ask for `WHERE entry_id > :last ORDER BY entry_id LIMIT 1000`. The primary key index lets each batch seek straight to its start, so every batch costs the same, and a row can never be read twice. If the order were by created_at, the cursor would have to include entry_id as a tiebreaker in a row comparison, with an index on (created_at, entry_id).

deeper.body:
LATERAL does not always mean a loop. When the subquery has no LIMIT, no aggregate and no other reason to run per row, the planner can often pull it up into an ordinary join and choose a hash join, as it would for the same query written without LATERAL. The per-row plan appears when the subquery needs it, as LIMIT does. Read the plan: a Nested Loop with `loops` equal to the outer row count is the per-row form.

Going backward with a keyset cursor means flipping two things: the comparison and the sort. For the previous page, ask for `(created_at, payment_id) > (:first_created_at, :first_payment_id) ORDER BY created_at ASC, payment_id ASC LIMIT 20`, then reverse the 20 rows in the application. The same index serves both directions.

A total count, "page 3 of 51,231", is its own problem. `count(*)` over a million rows reads them all on every request, whatever pagination you use. Most interfaces do better with "more results" than with an exact total; when an estimate is enough, the planner's row estimate from EXPLAIN, or `reltuples` in pg_class for a whole table, costs nothing.

OFFSET has one more trap. With a locking clause, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE ... OFFSET 100`, the rows that OFFSET skips are locked too, though they are not returned. Lesson 13 builds job queues with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and LIMIT, never OFFSET.

Finally, every list query in this lesson, with or without a cursor, is only fast if an index matches its WHERE and ORDER BY in the right column order: equality columns first (card_id), then the sort key (created_at, payment_id). Lesson 11 explains why that order matters, and how to read the plans that show it.
